title: Research
text:
My first two first-author papers in Plant and Soil examine how young temperate trees adjust their fine-root systems to contrasting growing-season water availability. The first showed that species differed in their adjustments of absorptive fine-root biomass and rooting depth, while the second revealed species-specific changes in root architecture and morphology, with root branching density emerging as an important response to low water availability. My current manuscript extends this work to root-associated fungi, examining how fungal communities respond to water availability and how their composition and functional groups relate to fine-root traits and tree growth.

title: About
text:
About me
I am a forest ecologist interested in how trees respond to environmental change below- and aboveground. My research focuses on the traits and processes that allow trees to adjust to changing water availability, especially fine-root morphology, carbon allocation, and interactions with soil fungi. I combine field experiments, root trait measurements, molecular methods, and quantitative analysis to understand why tree species differ in their responses and what those differences may mean for forest resilience.
